**German economy ends 2025 with marginal growth as stimulus hopes meet structural drag**

BERLIN – Germany's economy edged out of recession in 2025, but growth remained close to stagnation, leaving Europe's largest economy reliant on a government spending push to revive momentum.

Official figures showed gross domestic product expanded by roughly 0.2% for the year, following contractions in both 2023 and 2024. Output rose in the first quarter, fell in the second and was broadly flat in the third, reflecting weak exports and subdued investment.

U.S. tariffs weighed heavily on a manufacturing sector already struggling with high energy costs, rising competition from China and slow demand. A trade framework agreed between Washington and Brussels in the summer set a 15% levy on most European goods, offering clarity but not relief. The car industry, machinery makers and chemical producers announced further job cuts.

The labor market softened accordingly. Registered unemployment passed three million in August for the first time in a decade, although the figure partly reflected seasonal factors. Inflation, meanwhile, eased to around 2%, allowing the European Central Bank to hold its deposit rate at 2% after a series of cuts earlier in the year.

The most significant shift came in fiscal policy. Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who took office in May, won parliamentary approval for changes to the constitutional debt brake. The reform exempts most defense spending from borrowing limits and creates a 500-billion-euro fund for infrastructure and climate projects over 12 years.

Economists expect the measures to lift growth from 2026, but the timing is uncertain. Planning delays, labor shortages and bureaucratic hurdles could slow the flow of money into projects. Business groups also say that without lower energy costs, reduced red tape and tax reform, public spending alone will not restore competitiveness.

The government and leading institutes forecast a modest recovery next year, though risks remain, including trade tensions and weak global demand.

**German economy ekes out modest growth in 2025 as fiscal stimulus looms**

BERLIN – Germany's economy returned to slight growth in 2025 after two years of contraction, but weak industry, U.S. trade barriers and a softening labor market kept Europe's largest economy well short of a robust recovery.

Gross domestic product expanded by roughly 0.2% for the year, according to preliminary figures from the Federal Statistical Office. The economy had shrunk in both 2023 and 2024. Growth early in the year was followed by a dip in the second quarter and near stagnation in the third.

Exports, long the engine of the German model, faced headwinds from higher U.S. tariffs. A framework deal between Washington and the European Union in July set a 15% levy on most EU goods, lower than feared but still a burden for carmakers, machinery producers and chemical firms. Competition from China added to the pressure on manufacturers, and major companies in the auto and supplier sectors announced job cuts.

The labor market weakened. The number of people registered as unemployed rose above three million in August, the first time in about a decade, though the seasonally adjusted rate remained moderate by historical standards.

Inflation eased to around 2%, near the European Central Bank's target, supporting household purchasing power. The ECB held its deposit rate at 2% after a series of cuts.

The main source of optimism was fiscal policy. Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who took office in May, secured parliamentary approval in March for a constitutional change that loosened the "debt brake" for defense spending and created a 500 billion euro fund for infrastructure over 12 years. Spending from those programs has been slow to start, and economists say the effects will mostly arrive in 2026 and beyond.

Most forecasters expect growth of about 1% next year, provided public investment is delivered on schedule and global trade conditions do not worsen. Business groups continue to urge the government to cut energy costs, reduce bureaucracy and lower taxes to restore competitiveness.

Economists expect the measures to lift growth gradually from 2026, though disbursement has been slower than many anticipated. Business groups say spending must be matched by lower energy costs, reduced bureaucracy and tax reform to restore competitiveness.

**Germany's economy edges out of recession in 2025, but recovery remains fragile**

BERLIN – Germany's economy returned to marginal growth in 2025 after two years of contraction, as government spending plans and a steadier consumer offset weak industry and trade pressure, official data and economists' assessments show.

The Federal Statistical Office reported that gross domestic product rose by roughly 0.2 percent for the year, following declines of 0.9 percent in 2023 and 0.5 percent in 2024. The result left Europe's largest economy among the weakest performers in the euro area.

The year began with a modest expansion in the first quarter, driven partly by exporters shipping goods ahead of new U.S. tariffs. Output then slipped in the second quarter and stagnated in the third as the duties, including a 15 percent levy on most European Union goods under a July trade framework, weighed on manufacturers. Carmakers, machinery producers and chemical firms reported falling orders and continued job cuts.

The labor market softened. Registered unemployment passed three million in August for the first time in a decade, though the figure is partly seasonal and reflects a larger workforce. Inflation eased to an annual average of about 2.2 percent, giving households some relief, while the European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2 percent after a series of cuts.

Policy provided the main source of optimism. Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who took office in May, secured parliamentary approval for a constitutional change loosening the debt brake for defense spending and creating a 500 billion euro fund for infrastructure over twelve years. Spending from the package has been slow to start, and economists say its effects will largely be felt from 2026.

Forecasters expect growth of about 1 percent next year, contingent on faster project approvals, lower energy costs and stable trade relations. Business groups continue to call for reductions in bureaucracy, taxes and power prices to restore competitiveness.

**German economy ends 2025 with meager growth as stimulus hopes build**

BERLIN – Germany's economy edged out of recession in 2025, growing by only about two-tenths of a percent after two straight years of contraction, according to preliminary figures from the Federal Statistical Office.

Europe's largest economy was held back by weak industrial output, soft export demand and high energy costs. U.S. tariffs added to the strain. A trade deal reached in July between Washington and Brussels set a 15% duty on most European goods, which hit carmakers, machinery producers and chemical firms particularly hard.

The economy contracted in the second quarter, stagnated in the third, and showed only modest momentum toward year-end. Manufacturers announced thousands of job cuts. In August, unemployment passed 3 million for the first time in a decade, according to the Federal Labour Agency.

Consumer prices were steadier. Inflation hovered around 2%, in line with the European Central Bank's target, allowing the ECB to hold its deposit rate at 2% from mid-year. Household spending nonetheless remained cautious, with savings rates elevated amid job insecurity.

The main shift came in fiscal policy. Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who took office in May, secured parliamentary approval in March for a landmark reform of the constitutional debt brake. The change exempts most defense spending from borrowing limits and creates a €500 billion fund for infrastructure and climate projects over 12 years.

Spending from the package was slow to reach the economy in 2025, as contracts and planning approvals lagged. Economists say the effect should build gradually through 2026.

The government projects growth of about 1.3% next year, while the Bundesbank and several institutes are more cautious, warning that structural problems persist. These include an aging workforce, heavy bureaucracy, underinvestment in digital networks and rising competition from China.

"The stimulus is real, but it is not a cure-all," said one Frankfurt-based economist. "Reform of the business environment will determine whether this recovery lasts."

BERLIN – Germany's economy returned to marginal growth in 2025 after two years of contraction, but the expansion was too weak to mark a real turnaround for Europe's largest economy.

Gross domestic product rose by about two-tenths of a percent for the year, according to preliminary figures from the Federal Statistical Office. The result followed declines in 2023 and 2024 and left output roughly where it stood before the pandemic.

The labor market weakened. Registered unemployment passed 3 million in August for the first time in a decade, and manufacturers continued to cut jobs. Inflation, however, eased to around 2%, and the European Central Bank held its key rate steady after a series of cuts, giving households some relief.

The brightest development was fiscal. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition won parliamentary approval in March to loosen the constitutional debt brake for defense spending and to create a 500 billion euro fund for infrastructure and climate projects. Economists expect the money to lift growth gradually, although the rollout has been slower than the government promised.

Forecasters broadly predict a stronger 2026, with the government projecting growth above 1%. Many economists caution that the outlook depends on how quickly public funds reach projects, and on whether Berlin can pair spending with reforms to cut bureaucracy, ease labor shortages and lower energy costs.

BERLIN – Europe's largest economy ended 2025 with marginal growth, avoiding a third straight year of contraction but leaving its recovery dependent on a government spending push that has yet to take full effect.

The labor market softened accordingly. Registered unemployment passed 3 million in August, the first time in a decade. Inflation, meanwhile, hovered near 2%, and the European Central Bank held its key deposit rate at 2% after a series of cuts that ended in June, offering little further monetary support.

Hopes now rest on fiscal policy. Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who took office in May leading a coalition of conservatives and Social Democrats, secured a constitutional change in March that loosened the debt brake for defense spending and created a €500 billion infrastructure fund to be spent over 12 years. Defense orders have already lifted some manufacturers, including Rheinmetall, but money for roads, rail and digital networks has flowed slowly because of planning and permitting delays.

The government projects growth of 1.3% in 2026, while several private forecasters are more cautious. Economists say the outcome will depend on how quickly the stimulus is converted into orders and on whether global trade tensions ease.

BERLIN – Germany avoided a third straight year of contraction in 2025, but growth of roughly a fifth of a percentage point left Europe's largest economy far from a convincing recovery, according to official estimates.

The federal statistics office said output was held back by weak exports, sluggish industrial production and cautious consumers. Gains early in the year faded as trade tensions escalated, and activity flattened over the summer months.

U.S. tariffs weighed heavily on manufacturers. Washington and Brussels agreed in July on a 15% duty on most European goods, lower than feared but well above previous levels. Carmakers, machinery builders and chemical producers reported shrinking orders, and several announced job cuts. Competition from China added pressure, particularly in the auto sector.

The labor market weakened accordingly. Registered unemployment passed 3 million in August for the first time in a decade, though the figure reflected partly seasonal and structural factors, and employers continued to report shortages of skilled workers in some fields.

Inflation eased to around 2%, allowing the European Central Bank to bring its deposit rate down to 2% by June and hold it there. Real wage growth gave households some support, yet savings rates stayed high.

The biggest shift came from fiscal policy. In March, lawmakers approved changes to the constitutional debt brake, exempting most defense spending above a set threshold and creating a €500 billion fund for infrastructure over 12 years. Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who took office in May, has promised faster approvals, lower energy costs and reduced bureaucracy.

Economists said the spending would take time to feed through, with public investment and military procurement expected to lift activity gradually. Delays in awarding contracts, capacity limits in the construction sector and political disputes inside the governing coalition remain risks.

Leading institutes forecast moderate expansion in 2026, but warned that lasting growth would depend on structural reforms, not just higher public outlays.

Inflation eased to about 2.2% on average, allowing the European Central Bank to hold its deposit rate at 2% after a series of cuts.

The main source of optimism was fiscal policy. Disbursements were slow to start, but economists expect the stimulus to support growth from 2026.

His government, backed by a constitutional change to the debt brake, launched a 500 billion euro infrastructure fund spread over 12 years and opened the way for much higher defense spending. Economists broadly expect the measures to lift activity, though disbursement has been slower than promised, and bureaucratic hurdles remain.

BERLIN – Germany's economy barely grew in 2025, ending a two-year contraction but falling well short of a robust recovery, as weak exports, high energy costs and U.S. tariffs weighed on Europe's largest economy.

Output expanded only by a fraction of a percent for the year, according to preliminary estimates from the Federal Statistical Office. Activity was uneven. A solid first quarter, boosted by front-loaded exports ahead of U.S. tariffs, gave way to a contraction in the second quarter and near stagnation in the months that followed.

Manufacturing remained the main drag. Carmakers, chemical firms and machinery producers faced weaker demand from China, tougher competition and higher costs than rivals in the United States and Asia. Volkswagen and other major industrial groups continued to announce job cuts. In August, registered unemployment climbed above 3 million for the first time in a decade, a symbolic threshold for a labor market that had long been a source of strength.

Inflation eased to roughly 2%, near the European Central Bank's target, giving households some relief. The ECB held its key rate at 2% after a series of cuts, offering limited extra support.

The government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, in office since May, pinned its hopes on fiscal policy. Parliament approved a landmark reform of the constitutional debt brake and created a 500 billion euro fund for infrastructure, alongside a sharp increase in defense spending. Economists say the effects will build gradually, as planning and procurement bottlenecks delay projects.

Trade policy added uncertainty. A framework deal between the European Union and Washington capped most U.S. tariffs on European goods at 15%, but exporters said the levies still squeezed margins and complicated investment decisions.

The government expects growth to pick up to 1.3% in 2026 as public spending takes hold. Many economists are more cautious, warning that structural problems, including an aging workforce, bureaucracy and high energy prices, will limit the rebound unless reforms follow.

BERLIN – Europe's largest economy limped through 2025, avoiding a third consecutive year of outright contraction but failing to deliver the recovery policymakers had hoped for.

Official data showed gross domestic product barely grew over the year, following declines in 2023 and 2024. Output rose early in the year as companies rushed to ship goods ahead of U.S. tariffs, then fell back in the second quarter as that demand faded.

Industry remained the weak spot. High energy costs, fierce competition from China and trade tensions with Washington weighed on carmakers, machinery producers and chemical firms. Inflation, by contrast, eased to roughly 2%, close to the European Central Bank's target. The ECB cut its deposit rate to 2% by mid-year and then held it steady, leaving borrowing costs lower but not low enough to spark a investment boom.

The most significant shift came from fiscal policy. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government, which took office in May, secured parliamentary approval to loosen the constitutional debt brake for defence spending and to create a 500 billion euro fund for infrastructure and climate projects over 12 years. Economists expect the spending to lift growth from 2026, though disbursement has been slower than ministers promised.

Business sentiment improved modestly late in the year but stayed fragile. Economists say lasting recovery will depend on whether the government can turn spending pledges into projects, cut bureaucracy and bring down energy and labour costs.

"The money is on the way, but the structural problems have not gone away," said one Frankfurt-based analyst.

**German economy edges out of stagnation in 2025 as fiscal stimulus looms**

BERLIN – Germany's economy returned to marginal growth in 2025 after two years of contraction, but the recovery remained fragile, weighed down by weak industry, trade tensions and structural challenges.

Preliminary figures from the Federal Statistical Office indicated gross domestic product rose about 0.2% for the year. The economy had shrunk in both 2023 and 2024, leaving Europe's largest economy as a laggard among major peers.

The year was uneven. Output expanded in the opening quarter, helped by exporters rushing shipments ahead of U.S. tariffs, then contracted in the spring and stagnated over the summer. Analysts said the pattern reflected front-loaded trade activity followed by a hangover once higher duties took hold.

Washington's tariff regime, including a 15% levy on most European Union goods under a July framework deal, hit carmakers, machinery producers and chemical firms hardest. Volkswagen, Bosch, ZF and other industrial names continued to announce job cuts as they grappled with high energy costs, Chinese competition and a slow shift to electric vehicles.

The labor market softened accordingly. Registered unemployment topped 3 million in August for the first time in more than a decade, though a shrinking workforce kept the jobless rate below levels seen in many neighboring countries.

Inflation eased to roughly 2%, allowing the European Central Bank to hold its deposit rate at 2% after a series of cuts. Consumers nonetheless stayed cautious, and household saving remained elevated.

The main source of optimism was fiscal. Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who took office in May, pushed through a constitutional reform in March loosening the debt brake for defense spending and creating a 500 billion euro infrastructure fund spread over 12 years. Spending is expected to build gradually, with the strongest effects anticipated in 2026.

The government projects growth of about 1.3% next year, while several independent institutes are more cautious, citing slow project approvals, bureaucratic hurdles and uncertainty over global trade.

For now, economists say, Germany has stopped shrinking but has yet to prove it can sustain a durable upswing.
